newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU salmon duty would be big blow, Norway says.
newsitem.headline: EU salmon duty would be big blow, Norway says.

text.p: Norway's salmon industry would suffer a major blow if the European Commission imposed punitive anti-dumping duties on EU imports of farmed Norwegian salmon, Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal said on Wednesday.
Godal, speaking after inconclusive talks with EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan on the trade row, said parts of the country's salmon industry could probably survive.

"But it would be a major strike against the industry in general," Godal told reporters. He reiterated Oslo's desire for dialogue to solve the dispute, rather than confrontation through unilateral trade measures.
Norway's salmon exports to the European Union are worth some 5.5 billion crowns ($790 million) annually.

The EU executive is considering an average duty of 13.7 percent on Norwegian salmon imports, accusing the country's producers of receiving state subsidies and dumping the fish on the EU market at less than the cost of production.
Scottish and Irish competitors say Norway, the world's biggest producer, is flooding the market and depressing prices.
Norway, which like the European Union is part of the 18-nation European Economic Area, strongly rejects the allegations, saying Scottish producers have actually increased their market shares.
"We can hardly see that we have caused injury to the European salmon market," Godal said.
The trade conflict is seen in Norway as the most serious dispute with the European Union since Norwegians rejected membership of the bloc in a 1994 referendum.
Norway had taken steps to restrict production and was prepared to discuss more measures, Godal said without elaborating.
But there were no signs that the salmon duties would be part of an EU trade offensive against Oslo as industry has suggested, Godal said.
Godal and Fisheries Minister Karl Eirik Schuett-Pedersen had already met EU External Affairs Commissioner Hans van den Broek on Monday before Wednesday's talks with Brittan.
Brittan gave no indication that he might change his view. "Actually, we did not expect that Sir Leon would solve the matter here today," Godal said.

But he said he hoped that opposition among several EU member states to the idea of the salmon duties would influence the decision of the Commission, although it has the power to impose provisional duties without the consent of member states.

On Tuesday, EU sources said some EU countries were critical of or had doubts about the Commission's proposal and one source said only Britain and Ireland -- which also farm salmon -- openly supported Brittan's recommendation.

Godal said he believed Norway had strengthened its position over the last few days, especially among EU member states. But Brittan's spokesman Peter Guilford said the commissioner's views would only be influenced by the merits of the arguments.
